w:r.w:t: THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 17, 2026 / GAS STATION + CONVENIENCE STORE
Qualify the location. Make the proposition clear. Leave with a specific next step.
The goal is not to sell campaign software or promise a launch date. The goal is to determine whether this store can support a worthwhile, reliable four-week pilot.

“Uptick is a free local membership that helps nearby people discover something useful at participating convenience stores. Members get a featured perk with no purchase required. You provide an agreed item and a simple counter process; Uptick manages the member experience and records the response. I’d like to understand what you want people to discover here and whether a bounded four-week test makes sense.”
Suggested language, not a claim that this store, its inventory, or a paying program has already been approved.

Identify the person who can commit the store. Select one candidate item and a practical substitute. Obtain real unit cost, weekly capacity, staffed hours, and a manager contact. Agree a counter rehearsal and a follow-up to settle the program scope and negotiated fee.

This is a September 14, 2026 snapshot taken after the final pre-pilot software campaign. The release path was repaired and re-verified: the automated suite passes in full, including separate-session PostgreSQL contention on an isolated cluster, and the production build succeeds. Enrollment stays closed, no real member exists, and no real text message is sent. Hosted commissioning, carrier messaging approval, and the physical counter rehearsal remain open. Demonstrate the verified internal environment on Thursday and describe a pilot that is ready to be scheduled, not a live public service. [1]
Private founder preparation. Do not forward this packet as a merchant agreement or use it as a release certificate.
Ask about the store before walking through the platform. Record the owner’s answers as statements to verify, not automatically as operational proof.
Who can approve the program fee, inventory commitment, cashier instructions, and any changes? Who manages the participating shifts?
What do you most want nearby people to discover: the store, coffee, breakfast, a stocked product, or a quieter time of day?
Who uses the store now? What do you know about people who buy fuel but do not enter? What evidence supports that?
Would the proposed item be useful without a fuel purchase? Is the stop convenient for people living or working nearby?
Which SKU or size can you offer consistently? Is there a useful non-caffeinated option or acceptable substitute?
What is the landed cost per fulfilled item, including cup, packaging, waste, and any extra handling?
What weekly quantity could you honor if every reserved benefit is used? How will stock be replenished and protected?
Which hours have trained staff? Can they recognize the pass, present the staff QR, and hand over the item without confusion?
What happens if the machine breaks, stock runs out, the cashier refuses, or the location closes? Who answers immediately?
Do you already have loyalty, supplier promotions, or operating restrictions that this program must not conflict with?
What would make a paid renewal worthwhile? What can you measure without treating every redemption as a new customer or sale?
Who will confirm the proposed item, cost, capacity, and staff process? Can we agree the counter rehearsal and follow-up date?
Stop or redesign the proposal if the store cannot commit authority, a genuinely free item, trained staff, realistic stock, or a usable failure response.
Discuss a bounded pilot, not unlimited demand

The current planning baseline is a four-week Market Cell with 150 target admitted adults and a 200-member cap. That is a cell-level target, not an existing audience or a guarantee that every member visits this station. [2]
Discussion entry — not agreed until confirmed
[NONE OR EXPLICIT CATEGORY / RADIUS / DATES / EXCEPTIONS]

Maximum primary reward exposure = total committed units × agreed direct fulfillment cost. Add the Growth fee and any additional operating costs separately. Identify recovery exposure rather than hiding it in the primary item cost.
At 150 members across four weeks, the network promise is 600 member-weeks. This does not mean 600 benefits at this location, 600 views, or 600 incremental sales.
Do not turn a discussion into a promise

A supplier may contribute useful benefits without buying Growth; that does not guarantee distribution. Paid Growth has an agreed scope and fee. Hosting a screen is optional. Any protection is limited to the explicit paid-featured scope and must not eliminate organic participation or member recovery. [2]
A free rehearsal is different from a commercial pilot. Keep proposed price, agreed price, invoice, payment, and benefit exposure distinct.
Show a real workflow, with a safe fallback

Only demonstrate an environment that the technical owner has actually verified. Use clearly labeled sample/internal data. Do not create real member obligations or send real promotional messages to make the meeting look live.
“This is a rehearsal of the pilot workflow. The real location, stock, staff process, and launch checks must still be confirmed.”
Show the private member flow and optional promotional checkbox. Declining marketing must not remove membership or a committed benefit.
Show one exact item, location, usable hours, no-purchase terms, and expiry. Explain what is reserved and what is not.
Show claim, staff-presented QR, and the fresh completion screen. Explain that staff still needs to hand over the item.
Show an actual tested stockout or failed-handoff recovery. Keep the original attempt visible; do not manufacture a successful handoff.
Show the agreed program, stock obligations, observed activity, incidents/recovery, and fee/credits. Do not display member phone lists.
When the connection or demo fails

Use screenshots or a short PDF captured from the verified build, clearly marked REHEARSAL. Walk through the same six steps. Never present a mockup of unfinished functionality as a functioning feature.
The three statements to get right
“Recorded redemption” is not independent proof of a purchase or physical handoff.
“Target 150 members” is not “we already have 150 customers for you.”
“Ready for a demonstration” is not “ready to launch to the public.”

Confirm the exact demo URL or local instructions, login, sample data, and offline fallback. Test the actual device and browser. Remove private records from view. Keep enrollment, real SMS, and account protections in their intended states.

The hosted record still separates anonymous access checks from successful authenticated hosted journeys, and real-phone and counter testing remain unfinished. The member benefit, claim, staff-QR redemption and failure-recovery paths are verified locally against a real database, so demonstrate those from the verified internal environment and say plainly that the hosted public service is not yet commissioned. Answer plainly; do not sell around the truth

“That may already serve your regular customers. This test focuses on introducing a relevant local membership to something worth discovering here. We should first establish whether it adds anything to your existing setup.”
“They will only come for free items.”
“Some may. That is a risk we need to measure, not dismiss. We will keep the commitment bounded and review repeat use, your operating cost, and your willingness to continue.”
“The fee pays for the agreed managed program; the item creates the member value. Both costs should be visible. If the likely value does not justify them, we should not pretend the program works.”
“Then we need to simplify and rehearse it with the people serving customers. We will not launch an item that depends on a process staff cannot reliably follow.”
“Any paid-featured protection must specify the location, category, radius, dates, and exceptions. It is not permanent control over all nearby benefits, organic supply, or recovery.”
“No unrestricted member list. Uptick manages the membership relationship. You receive relevant program and fulfillment reporting, not permission to market independently to everyone.”
“We agree capacity and an actual substitute or replacement route before release. There is a named support owner and payer. We should solve the member’s problem first.”
“No. It records use of the configured redemption process. We will not label that as a verified purchase or claim that the program caused a sale without suitable evidence.”
“Not for the core free member benefit. Let’s see whether a genuinely free item can work within your capacity. Otherwise this may not fit the first pilot.”
“After the agreed supply, staff, member capacity, support, software, and messaging requirements are actually ready. Today we can agree the next concrete step.”
Close on an action, not enthusiasm

“Can we identify the item and substitute, confirm your cost and weekly capacity, and schedule a short counter rehearsal with the manager? Then we can settle the four-week scope and fee with both sides clear on what is being tested.”
Leave with facts, owners, and dates

Open with the store’s objective. Spend most of the conversation on its customers, product economics, and counter reality. Show the verified workflow only after establishing fit. Finish by recording a specific rehearsal, information request, or commercial follow-up. This is an agenda suggestion, not the confirmed meeting length.
[PROCEED TO REHEARSAL / REVISE / NOT A FIT]
Subject: Next steps for the Uptick pilot discussion
Thanks for meeting today. The opportunity we discussed was [OBJECTIVE] at [LOCATION].
We agreed that [PERSON] will confirm [ITEM, COST, CAPACITY OR HOURS] by [DATE], and the next step is [COUNTER REHEARSAL OR FOLLOW-UP] on [DATE].

The proposed four-week scope is [SCOPE]. The fee, final quantities, launch date, and any protection remain [PROPOSED / AGREED AS SPECIFIED]. We will confirm the operational and launch requirements before inviting members to use a benefit at the store.
Please correct anything I have misunderstood.
Draft only. Do not send automatically. Remove terms that were not discussed, and never describe a proposal as an agreement.

Confirm the owner/attendee, address, and meeting time. Review the latest readiness statement. Test the demo and offline fallback. Bring the scope worksheet and reviewed merchant one-pager. Know the single next step you are asking for. Do not arrive relying on an untested login or an assumed agreement.
From an interested owner to a real pilot
Confirm exact item, usable hours, authority, trained shifts, stock/replenishment, independent fallback, support owner/backup, negotiated commercial terms, and actual partner distribution.
Reconfirm current stock, staff, hours, QR, and fallback. Review member-to-store usefulness, full-cohort backing, and paid limits. Do not assume last week’s readiness proves this week.
Handle known failures first. Check support and unresolved remedies, delivery uncertainty, partner actions, and changes in staff/stock. Record actual operating time and cost.
Stop directing additional people into the same unresolved problem. Contact the manager. Arrange a backed remedy and record who pays. Never change a failed handoff into a false success.
Keep the original cohort in the analysis. Obtain a real renew/repair/stop decision. Reconcile money and work. Decide how membership continues or pauses before the pilot quietly expires.

First use: 75 members. Use in two or more distinct weeks: 45. Week-four use: at least 38. These are provisional management targets, not proven benchmarks, sales guarantees, or causal evidence. Record digital use separately from confirmed fulfillment. [3]

Also ask: Were all admitted member-weeks backed? Did the partner actually distribute? Were failures repaired? Will a merchant pay to continue? Can another person operate the cell? Does the business work when benefits are used and labor is counted?
